newsitem.title: USA: Dole backs chemical weapons pact as Senate debates.
newsitem.headline: Dole backs chemical weapons pact as Senate debates.

text.p: The Senate debated an international treaty outlawing chemical weapons on Wednesday as supporters hailed endorsement of the treaty by last year's Republican presidential candidate, Bob Dole.
In a series of speeches, conservative Republicans attacked the Chemical Weapons Convention as a worse than useless document that could increase the threat of poison gas.
Its defenders said that while it was not perfect it would enhance U.S. security and provide a tool to reduce the threat of chemical warfare and terrorism.

After a rare closed session to discuss intelligence issues, the Senate will decide in a series of votes on Thursday whether the United States will join more than 70 other countries in ratifying the treaty.

Dole's surprise appearance at a White House rally for the Chemical Weapons Convention was a major coup for President Bill Clinton. He has put his foreign policy credibility on the line in an all-out lobbying campaign for the treaty.
The 1993 convention bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons. It goes into effect next Tuesday, with or without the United States.
It was Dole who, in the midst of the presidential campaign last September, wrote a letter to Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott raising questions about the treaty.

Fearing this would plunge the pact into election-year politics and doom it to defeat, the administration asked that it be pulled from the Senate floor. Dole said on Wednesday that 28 clarifications agreed to by the administration took care of his earlier objections. The Senate adopted the agreed 28 conditions by voice vote.
"If I were present in the Senate (where he was former Republican leader), I would vote for the CWC because of the many improvements that have been agreed to," Dole said.

In fact, two issues Dole raised last September are still in dispute. Amendments upgrading standards of verifiability against cheating and requiring global membership in the treaty are expected to be struck out by treaty supporters.

Just before the Senate opened two days of debate, Lott, whose position is expected to influence uncommitted Republicans, said he was waiting to see "the final product" before making up his mind. He was careful not to foreclose the possibility that he would vote for the treaty and said he was in contact with the administration.
Lott told reporters that "a good dozen, at least" among the 55 Republican senators were undecided on the treaty.

The Council for a Liveable World, a pro-arms-control lobbying group, counted 57 votes for the treaty and 10 "leaning" towards. Assuming all senators vote, 67 will be needed to approve the pact. White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the administration was "close...not there yet."

Before the final vote, the Senate will decide, in simple majority votes, whether to strip out so-called "killer" amendments to the ratification resolution that would bar U.S. participation in the treaty.
Lott zeroed in on a treaty provision that appears to have become the crucial factor in prospects for ratification.

This is Article 11 under which parties to the treaty "undertake to facilitate, and have the right to participate in, the fullest possible exchange of chemicals, equipment and scientific and technical information" allowed by the treaty.

The article also requires parties not to restrict trade development and promotion of scientific knowledge of chemistry for peaceful purposes and to make their own national regulations consistent with the treaty.

The ratification resolution that emerged from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, headed by treaty archfoe Jesse Helms, would make U.S. ratification conditional on elimination of these clauses and total elimination of Article 10, calling for exchange of chemical arms defence technology.
Helms argues that what he calls the "poisons for peace" result in chemical weapons technology going to "rogue" states.
